passages.happening:
God tells Moses to give Israel the boundaries of the land. “When you enter the land of Canaan, it will be allotted to you as an inheritance with these boundaries” (verse 2).

The southern border runs from the end of the Salt Sea, south of Kadesh-barnea, to the Brook of Egypt and the sea (verses 3-5). The western border is ‘the coastline of the Great Sea’ (verse 6). The northern border runs from the Great Sea to Lebo-hamath and on to Hazar-enan (verses 7-9). The eastern border comes down past the Sea of Chinnereth and along the Jordan to the Salt Sea (verses 10-12). “This will be your land, defined by its borders on all sides” (verse 12).

Moses adds that this land is for nine and a half tribes, since Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh already have theirs east of the Jordan (verses 13-15).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 33 looked back over the road. This chapter draws the map of what lies ahead. For forty years Israel has been a people without a country. The promise first made to Abraham, ‘I will give this land to your offspring’ (Genesis 12:7), is here given edges.

The list goes round the land like the hands of a clock: south, west, north, east. Each side ends with the same kind of sentence. The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea. The Great Sea is the Mediterranean. The Sea of Chinnereth is the Sea of Galilee. The Brook of Egypt is usually identified with a dry riverbed in the north of the Sinai Peninsula. Some points on the northern line cannot be placed with certainty.

Descriptions of boundaries were a known form in the ancient world. They appear in treaties and in grants of land, where a great king set out the territory he was giving to someone under him. Here God is the great king, and he is making a grant. The key word is again ‘inheritance’. Israel will not simply take this land. It will receive it, as children receive a family holding from a father.

Many scholars have noticed that the northern and southern lines are close to the extent of Egypt's province of Canaan in the late Bronze Age, as Egyptian records describe it. The borders describe the land of Canaan as the world of that time knew it.

Israel never held all of this land in the time of the judges. The picture came nearest to being real under David and Solomon. And these are not the only borders the Bible gives. The promise to Abraham in Genesis 15 names a wider reach, and the prophet Ezekiel, in exile, drew the lines again in his own way. The Bible's own maps of the land differ from one another.

A reader should be clear about what this chapter is. It is a description of an inheritance promised to the tribes of ancient Israel on the eve of their entry. It is not a title deed to be laid on any map today, and these notes draw from it no conclusion about any modern nation, border or conflict. Christians hold differing views about the land and God's promises concerning it, and this note does not settle them.
passages.later:
At the dedication of the temple, Solomon's assembly is said to have come ‘from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt’ (1 Kings 8:65), the northern and southern limits named in this chapter.

The law protected the small borders too, the stones that marked one family's field: “You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker” (Deuteronomy 19:14).

The New Testament speaks of the promise in the widest terms. Paul says that Abraham was promised that he would be ‘heir of the world’ (Romans 4:13). And Hebrews says of Abraham and his family that ‘they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one’ (Hebrews 11:16).
passages.asks: After forty years with no fixed home, Israel was told exactly where home would be. Ask what promise of God you have held for a long time without seeing its shape. And ask whether you receive what you have as an inheritance from a Father, or hold it as something you took for yourself.

passages.t: The men who will divide it
passages.happening:
God names those who will share out the land. “These are the names of the men who are to assign the land as an inheritance for you: Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun” (verse 17). With them is to be one leader from each tribe (verse 18).

Ten names follow. The first is ‘Caleb son of Jephunneh from the tribe of Judah’ (verse 19).

“These are the ones whom the LORD commanded to apportion the inheritance to the Israelites in the land of Canaan” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter sets a place beside a list of people: a land with its borders, and the leaders who will hand it out.

The priest and the leader stand at the head, Eleazar and Joshua. The land will be shared out by lot, as chapter 26 laid down, and the lot was cast before God. So the priest is there as well as the commander. The sharing of the land is treated as an act done in God's presence, and not as a division of spoils.

Each tribe has its own leader present. No tribe will have its share decided in its absence.

The names belong to a new generation. Compare them with the leaders of chapter 1 and the scouts of chapter 13. None of those men is here, with one exception. Caleb, who stood against the ten at Kadesh, is named first among the tribal leaders. He and Joshua are the only two left of their generation, and they are the ones given charge of the inheritance. The men who believed that the land could be received are the men who give it out.

Several of the names carry the word el, God: Shemuel, Elidad, Kemuel, Pedahel. That was common in Israelite names.

The order of the tribes in the list roughly follows the order in which their lands would later lie, from south to north. The list is written by someone who can already see the tribes in their places.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua tells how it was done: “Now these are the portions that the Israelites inherited in the land of Canaan, as distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the tribes of Israel” (Joshua 14:1).

Jesus speaks of an inheritance given to those with no power to seize one: “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).
passages.asks: Caleb waited forty years, and his name stands first among those who gave out the land. Ask what long faithfulness of yours has not yet been answered. And ask whether, when you are trusted to share something out among others, you do it as one who will answer to God for it.
